scale: 0-10 integer, NA if the text gives no evidence bearing on the criterion
task: Each entry is a candidate criterion for judging machine-learning conference paper abstracts. Classify each as quality-relevant or incidental.

criteria.name: Applied-domain framing outside core machine learning
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how far the abstract is framed around an application domain outside core machine learning — medicine and clinical imaging, neuroscience and brain-computer interfaces, ecology and environment, field robotics, materials. Score domain framing only; core-ML work scores 0 regardless of quality.

criteria.name: Abstract length and verbosity
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how long and densely packed the abstract is compared with a typical conference abstract: 0 for a very short abstract of a few sentences, 10 for one that runs long with many clauses and sub-points. Judge extent only; do not judge whether the length is warranted.

criteria.name: Explanatory mechanism — says WHY the approach should work
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 how far the abstract states a causal or conceptual reason the proposed approach should succeed — an insight, hypothesis, or mechanism linking a design choice to the effect it is expected to produce. Score low when the abstract only lists what was built and then asserts that it performs well.

criteria.name: States the costs, limitations, or failure conditions of its own method
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract states any price paid for its gains — compute or memory overhead, a regime where the method degrades, a remaining unsolved part — rather than presenting an unqualified improvement.

criteria.name: Ambition of the claim together with the specificity of the evidence offered for it
criteria.instruction: Composite: first judge how large the abstract's central claim is (a field-level or community-level claim versus a narrow method claim), then judge how specific the evidence offered for that claim is; score 0-10 for the JOINT quality, giving high scores only when a big claim is matched by correspondingly concrete evidence and low scores when a big claim rests on vague evidence.

criteria.name: Theoretical claims tied to the proposed method with stated scope
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether any theory in the abstract is about the specific method or phenomenon at hand and its scope or assumptions are indicated (setting, model class, regime), rather than a generic mention that guarantees exist. Score NA when the abstract makes no theoretical claim at all.

criteria.name: Reframing — recasts the problem in a different formalism or abstraction
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 how far the work re-describes a familiar problem inside a different formalism, abstraction, or level of description (rather than adding a component to the standard formulation). Score high when the abstract names both the old framing and the new one it substitutes.

criteria.name: Branded method name or acronym
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the work brands itself with a coined capitalised name or acronym for its method, system, dataset, or benchmark, and repeats that name through the abstract. Score the branding practice only.

criteria.name: Motivation explains why the problem is hard, not merely that it is unaddressed
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the opening motivation gives a substantive reason the problem resists existing approaches (a stated obstacle, tension, or structural difficulty), as opposed to noting only that it is understudied, underexplored, or that a gap exists.

criteria.name: Breadth and diversity of the empirical evaluation actually enumerated
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 by how many genuinely distinct evaluation settings the abstract actually names — different tasks, benchmarks, modalities, languages, or model families — counting only settings that are stated, not promised. Score low when the evidence is one dataset or one task family.

criteria.name: Technical specificity — the method's objects and operations are named precisely
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on how precisely the abstract names the actual objects and operations of its method (what is parameterised, what is optimised, what is conditioned on what), such that a reader in the area could sketch the method's shape from the abstract alone. Score low for descriptions built out of generic nouns like framework, module, mechanism, strategy, and knowledge.

criteria.name: Contributions are separable components each with a stated role
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract decomposes its contribution into distinct parts and says what each part is for, so a reader can tell which piece does which job. Score low when parts are listed but their individual purpose is not stated, and NA when there is only a single undivided contribution.

criteria.name: Enumerated list formatting inside the abstract
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract is organised as an explicit enumerated list — numbered or parenthesised items, 'First/Second/Finally' scaffolding, bulleted contributions. Score the formatting only, regardless of what the items say.

criteria.name: Raw LaTeX or markup residue left in the abstract
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much unrendered markup survives in the abstract text: LaTeX commands, math delimiters left as literal characters, escaped percent or backslash characters, footnote markers, markdown emphasis. Score the residue only, not the content it decorates.

criteria.name: Diagnoses a specific failure mode of prior work with stated evidence
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract identifies a concrete, named defect in existing approaches and gives some stated basis for the diagnosis (an analysis, an observation, a theoretical argument), as opposed to asserting that prior work is limited or insufficient.

criteria.name: Magnitude of the engineering or data resource the work required
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on how much construction effort the abstract evidences — corpora built, systems trained at multiple scales, pipelines assembled, annotations collected — judged from what is described as having been made, not from claims about importance.

criteria.name: Reports a surprising, negative, or self-undercutting finding
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract reports at least one result that runs against the expected or convenient direction — a method that fails, a baseline that unexpectedly wins, a widely held assumption contradicted, or the authors' own approach falling short somewhere.

criteria.name: Density of promotional superlatives and hype vocabulary
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how heavily the abstract uses promotional vocabulary — remarkable, impressive, striking, significant, substantial, superior, novel, state-of-the-art, comprehensive, extensive. Count the promotional register, not whether the claims are true.

criteria.name: Generality demonstrated beyond the primary setting rather than asserted
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract shows the contribution working outside the setting it was designed for — a second architecture, a second domain, a much larger scale — as reported evidence. Score low when generality is only claimed ('plug-and-play', 'can be applied to any ...') without a reported case.

criteria.name: Topic sits in a currently dominant research area
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how central the abstract's subject is to the areas that currently dominate machine-learning publishing — large language models, multimodal or vision-language models, diffusion and other generative models, agents. Score topic membership only; a careful paper on an unfashionable topic should score low here.

criteria.name: Quantified headline result against a named baseline or prior record
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the abstract's central empirical claim is given as a specific number placed against a specifically named baseline, prior system, or record (e.g. 'X to Y on benchmark Z', '+N points over method M'). Score low for unquantified claims such as 'achieves state-of-the-art performance' or numbers with no stated comparison point.

criteria.name: Famous benchmark and dataset name-dropping
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 by how many widely recognised benchmark or dataset names the abstract mentions (for example ImageNet, CIFAR, COCO, SuperGLUE, WMT, MNIST, LibriSpeech, Atari). Count recognisable names only; do not judge whether the evaluation is appropriate.

criteria.name: Human or expert judgment used as evaluation evidence
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the evaluation includes judgments by people (human raters, domain experts, user studies, expert-annotated ground truth) rather than resting entirely on automatic metrics. Score by what the abstract states was actually collected.

criteria.name: Anonymized-repository or release-on-acceptance code boilerplate
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 by how prominently the abstract carries submission-time artifact boilerplate: an anonymised repository link (for example an anonymous code-hosting URL or a placeholder), or a promise that code or data will be released later or upon publication. Score 0 when no such statement appears; score by presence and prominence of the boilerplate, not by whether sharing is a good practice.

criteria.name: Signals of industrial-scale compute or frontier proprietary models
criteria.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the abstract signals access to large-scale industrial resources: named proprietary frontier models used or compared against, explicit GPU counts or cluster scale, model sizes in billions of parameters, corpora at hundreds of millions of items. Score the resource signal only.
